I read the short page first, then went to the record, the way the study asked.

The flat miss is 'health and energy' filed under matters that read well. This is the man who was diagnosed with a pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor in October 2003, delayed conventional surgery for nine months while he tried diet-based treatment, had the Whipple procedure in July 2004, took medical leave in January 2009 for a liver transplant that April, took another leave in January 2011, resigned as CEO that August, and was dead five weeks later at 56. There is no reading of that life in which health and energy comes out on the favourable side.

The page also contradicts itself in a way I've apparently seen before in this study: it lists 'spending, time away from home, and inner life' under matters that read hard, then two paragraphs later says the chart is 'unusually positive about spending, time away from home, and inner life, marriage and partnerships and long illness' - the same three items, called hard and then flagged as an unusual positive, in the same short page. You can't have it both ways. Taking the second, more specific claim at its word: inner life and marriage/partnerships land close to true - he had an unusually serious, decades-long private Zen Buddhist practice for a tech executive, and an unusually stable 20-year marriage to Laurene Powell for someone of his profile. Spending does not land true - NeXT burned through investor money for years on the black-cube factory and it nearly sank the company. And 'long illness' being flagged as a positive is simply the same miss as the health line, restated.

'Money and family life' reading well is half right: the money is not in question (Apple, then the 2006 Disney-Pixar stock making him Disney's largest individual shareholder), but 'family life' erases the fact that he denied paternity of his first daughter Lisa for close to two years before reconciling. 'Marriage and partnerships,' 'work and standing,' and 'income, gains and friends' reading well are the closest things to real hits - and unremarkable ones, since they'd read well for most successful, married public figures. The temperament line ('responsive and changeable, guided a good deal by feeling') is the kind of statement that fits nearly anyone and I would have said the same about a stranger.

Worth paying for? No - one real, verifiable hit (health flatly wrong, in fact) sits right next to a page that argues with itself about the very same three topics.
